input:
A drug in solution decomposes by first-order kinetics, which means that the rate of loss of the drug at any moment is proportional to the amount of the drug still present, and the concentration ratio follows the relation $$\ln\frac{C}{C_0} = -k t$$ where the rate constant $k$ for this decomposition is 0.111 min⁻¹. The question addressed here is how much of the drug remains after 93 min. Because the exponent in the relation is the product of the rate constant and the elapsed time, and that product is large for the time considered, the exponential term falls to a very small value, and the fraction remaining after the stated time is 0, at the precision of the stated value. In other words, for practical purposes the decomposition is essentially complete within the period considered, even though the first-order relation itself never quite reaches zero in a mathematical sense. One limitation of the result should be kept in mind: the rate constant was measured at one temperature, and no activation energy is available, so the calculation cannot be extended to other temperatures, where the rate constant would in general be different and the time for decomposition would change accordingly.

The result can also be read directly from the size of the exponent. When the product of the rate constant and the time is small, a substantial fraction of the drug survives in solution; when the product is large, very little survives, and the stated case falls firmly in the second of those two regimes, which is why the reported fraction is so small.

A drug in solution decomposes by first-order kinetics: the rate of loss at any moment is proportional to the amount still present. The concentration ratio is given by $$\ln\frac{C}{C_0} = -k t$$ The rate constant $k$ is 0.111 min⁻¹. After 93 min, the fraction remaining is 0, at the precision of the stated value. The exponent is the product of the rate constant and the elapsed time, and the product is large at the stated time. The exponential term is therefore very small, and decomposition is complete for practical purposes within the period considered. The first-order relation itself approaches zero without reaching it; the stated fraction is a rounded value, not an exact zero. The rate constant was measured at one temperature, and no activation energy is available. The calculation is limited to the measured temperature. At another temperature the rate constant differs, the time for decomposition changes with it, and no figure for another temperature can be obtained from the stated data.

The size of the exponent decides the outcome in general. A small product of rate constant and time leaves a substantial fraction of the drug in solution. A large product leaves very little. The stated case falls in the second regime, and the fraction remaining is minute before rounding. Presentation of the result depends on precision: a value carried to more decimal places would show a small residue, while the value at the stated precision is the figure reported here.
